"Fitting a model" sounds like a single act. It is really a search. The algorithm scores
how wrong the model currently is, changes the parameters to make that score a little
smaller, and repeats until further changes stop helping. Each page in this section takes
one part of that loop, on the same simulated survey as the rest of the course:

- **loss functions**, the score being made smaller, and how squared and absolute error
  draw different lines through the same stations;
- **finding the parameters**, by a formula for a few models and by a search for the rest;
- **gradient descent**, the simplest search, and why it needs standardised inputs;
- **maximum likelihood**, where each loss comes from: name the distribution behind the
  data, and the loss follows;
- **priors and ridge regression**, a penalty on the parameters that is a belief about
  them written into the loss;
- **checking a fit**, the signs that a search stopped early, had no lowest point or gives
  a different answer each run.

The section also pays back debts from earlier ones.
[Scaling and encoding](../02-marine-data/scaling-and-encoding.qmd) asked you to
standardise inputs without giving the full reason, and
[Gradient descent](gradient-descent.qmd) supplies it. Section 3's
[polynomial regression](../03-supervised-learning/linear-and-polynomial-regression.qmd)
predicted a negative count, and [Maximum likelihood](maximum-likelihood.qmd) shows that
squared error assumes a Normal response, which allows one. The penalty that
[5 · Generalisation and model complexity](../05-generalisation/index.qmd) uses to stop models overfitting
is the prior from [Priors and ridge regression](map-and-priors.qmd).
